newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget deal opponents maneuver for year 2000.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget deal opponents maneuver for year 2000.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton and Republican leaders may struggle to impose a budget deal on their parties, as politicians on both sides take positions designed to boost their presidential prospects for 2000.
"Whatever the deal is, the left of the Democratic Party and the right of the Republican Party will be up in arms," said political analyst Stephen Hess of the Brookings Institution.
"The question is one of leadership. If the leaders who shake hands on the deal can't make it stick, we may as well give up and try another system of government," he said.

Polls have consistently found the idea of balancing the budget is overwhelmingly popular with voters. Support often drops, however, when people realise how specific programmes they they value may be affected.

Clinton may have the tougher task of persuading Democrats to go along with cuts in social programmes while granting a capital gains tax that will mainly benefit the wealthy. Additionally, Democratic leaders are peeved that they were essentially cut out of budget negotiations.
With Clinton riding high in polls, Republicans in Congress could boost their standings and lay to rest criticism that they have been a do-nothing legislature by passing the budget.
According to a mid-April Gallup poll, only 30 percent approved of Congress's performance and 59 percent disapproved. Clinton's approval ratings have been in the mid-fifties.

The burden will fall on Clinton, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott to rally supporters during a legislative battle, likely to last most of the summer, to win approval for the budget.

Liberals will oppose cuts in social programmes like Medicare and Medicaid as well as tax cuts they say will mainly benefit the rich. Fiscal conservatives were already saying the accord left spending levels too high and tax cuts too low.

Even before the deal was announced, prospective Republican presidential candidates Jack Kemp and Steve Forbes had signed a letter and Forbes launched three radio advertisements opposing the agreement.
"Clinton's budget is really a $23 billion tax increase. Promising a tax cut when it's really a tax increase -- that's Clintonomics," said one ad.

"It's time to pass an honest budget, with a big income tax cut. Let's help families keep more of what they earn, help our economy grow and create new revenue to help balance the budget," said another.
On the Democratic side, House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, who is positioning himself to challenge Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination, made threatening noises.

"Obviously the administration has to work with a Republican majority. I understand that. We don't have the majority, they do," Gephardt said. "But we have a pretty healthy minority. We've got 207 votes here, and Democrats have strong feelings about these issues."

Gregory Valliere, managing director of the Washington Research Group, which provides Wall Street investors with political analysis, said a budget battle would be a foretaste of some of the themes of the 2000 presidential campaign.
"The campaign for 2000 begins in earnest today. Everybody will shoot at this agreement. But I assume the votes will be there to get it through," he said.
American University political scientist Allan Lichtman said: "The players for 2000 are all lining up in their expected dance positions."

The agreement places Gore in a particularly sensitive position. On the one hand, he may benefit if the agreement goes through and ends up helping the U.S. economy. On the other, he does not want to lose ground among traditional Democratic constituencies including labour unions that are being energetically courted by Gephardt.

"Gephardt will see this as an opportunity to appeal to Democratic constituences like organised labour. Gore's best bet will be to keep a low profile and let Clinton absorb the anger of the left," said Gary Jacobson, a political scientist at the University of California, San Diego.
